strengths: Timely and well-motivated exploration: Transitioning drag-based image editing from legacy UNet/DDPM architectures (e.g., SD 1.5/2.1) to modern Diffusion Transformers trained with flow matching (FLUX) is an important and relevant direction.

Insightful analysis of feature representations: The paper clearly identifies why classical point-based motion supervision fails on DiT backbones, demonstrating the distinction between the broad, compressed receptive fields of UNet bottlenecks and the fine-grained, localized token features of DiTs.

Methodological cohesion: The combination of progressive region-level affine supervision, hard background constraints, and adapter-enhanced inversion systematically tackles specific failure modes of DiTs and CFG distillation drift.

Comprehensive benchmark contribution: The introduction of ReD Bench (120 annotated samples with task tags, anchor points, and region masks) addresses clear limitations in existing drag editing benchmarks.
weaknesses: Factual and reproducibility concern regarding external dependencies: Section 3.2 and the bibliography cite 'GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025)' with a non-existent URL ('https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-5/'). As GPT-5 has not been released, this raises significant questions regarding experimental authenticity and reproducibility. The authors must clarify which MLLM was actually used (e.g., GPT-4o) and correct this claim.

Confounding base model capabilities in baseline comparisons: In Table 2, DragFlow (built upon FLUX.1-dev, ~12B parameters) is compared against prior methods predominantly built upon SD 1.5 / SD 2.1 (~1B parameters). While the paper aims to unleash FLUX priors, the lack of comparisons against other methods ported to FLUX—or evaluating the proposed region-based paradigm on SD—makes it difficult to fully isolate whether the quantitative gains come from the algorithmic contributions or simply the vastly superior base generator.

Increased user interaction complexity: Point-based drag editing gained popularity because users only need to provide pairs of source and target points. In contrast, DragFlow requires source region scribbles/masks, target centroids, anchor points for rotation, and user interaction to select from MLLM-generated candidate prompts. This shifts the interaction paradigm closer to localized inpainting/composition rather than minimal-click dragging.

Missing runtime and efficiency benchmarks: Iterative latent optimization through backpropagation on a 12B DiT model (70 iterations + dual reconstruction branches) is computationally demanding. The paper does not report latency, per-image editing time, or GPU VRAM requirements compared to baselines.

strengths: Timely and relevant focus: The paper tackles the challenging problem of adapting interactive drag-based image editing from legacy UNet architectures to modern Diffusion Transformers (DiTs, specifically FLUX.1-dev with flow matching).

Insightful problem identification: The analysis of feature representations between UNet (spatially compact, large receptive fields) and DiT (finer-grained, spatially localized) provides a convincing conceptual justification for why standard point-based motion supervision and point tracking degrade when naively applied to DiTs.

Comprehensive technical pipeline: The combination of progressive region-level affine supervision, hard gradient-masked background constraints, and adapter-enhanced inversion constitutes a complete and well-motivated framework.

Thorough ablation study: Table 3 and Figure 6 clearly isolate the impact of individual design components (region-level supervision, background preservation, and adapter integration) starting from a point-based FLUX baseline, validating their individual contributions.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons: The baselines compared in Table 2 (e.g., DragDiffusion, FreeDrag, DragLoRA, GoodDrag) are built upon older UNet backbones (e.g., SD 1.5/2.1), while DragFlow utilizes FLUX.1-dev (~12B parameters). Consequently, the significant improvements in visual realism and perceptual fidelity are heavily confounded by the capacity of the underlying generative model rather than the drag algorithm alone.

High pipeline complexity and external dependencies: The method requires multiple disparate modules: FLUX.1-dev, FireFlow inversion, an open-domain personalization adapter (InstantCharacter / IP-Adapter), and a proprietary multimodal LLM (GPT-5 / MLLM) to infer user intent and produce prompts. This significantly limits ease of use, cost-effectiveness, and self-containment compared to existing lightweight dragging methods.

Missing computational overhead and latency analysis: Performing 70 iterations of backpropagation through a 12B parameter DiT along with dual-branch reconstruction and inversion is computationally intensive. The paper lacks runtime and GPU memory benchmarks, which are critical for interactive image editing systems.

Limited flexibility for non-rigid deformations: The formulation relies fundamentally on progressive affine transformations (relocation, rotation, scaling/edge shifts). For complex, non-rigid topological deformations or organic non-affine structural changes, affine-based mask propagation may be overly restrictive or unnatural.

strengths: Timely and insightful investigation into adapting drag-based manipulation to modern Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) and rectified flow models (FLUX.1), moving beyond legacy UNet-based Stable Diffusion backbones.

Convincing diagnostic analysis (Section 3.1, Figure 2) explaining why point-based supervision struggles on DiT feature representations due to narrower receptive fields and fine-grained feature granularity.

Principled method design: replacing point tracking with progressive region-level affine supervision provides stable gradients, while hard background replacement and adapter-enhanced inversion effectively mitigate inversion drift in distilled rectified flow models.
Comprehensive experimental validation against nine competitive baselines across both DragBench-DR and the newly curated ReD Bench, supported by clear ablation studies.
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead: optimizing noisy latents across 70 steps through the 12B FLUX.1 model, running an additional reconstruction branch, and loading an identity adapter (InstantCharacter) likely entails high latency and VRAM requirements; however, inference time and memory comparisons with baselines are not reported.

Increased interaction complexity compared to classic drag-and-drop: the workflow requires drawing source masks, picking target points, specifying rotation anchors, and participating in a multi-step MLLM prompt selection step, which blurs the boundary between interactive drag-editing and regional inpainting/composition.

The paper cites and claims usage of 'GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025)' in Section 3.2 and Appendix D.3; this appears to be either an unreleased model, an inaccurate citation, or a hallucinated version name (e.g., GPT-4o). Additionally, the ablation does not evaluate performance when MLLM assistance/prompting is removed.
The newly introduced ReD Bench is relatively small (120 images), which somewhat limits the statistical diversity of the quantitative benchmarks.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated exploration: While generative vision has largely shifted to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) and rectified flow matching, drag-based image editing has remained predominantly confined to UNet-based models. This paper fills an important gap by pioneering drag editing on modern DiTs.

Insightful architectural analysis: The paper provides a clear and convincing explanation of why naive point-based drag fails on DiTs, identifying the narrower receptive field and fine-grained feature representation of DiTs (versus the highly compressed bottleneck features of UNets) as well as CFG-distillation drift as the primary failure modes.

Sound and effective methodology: The proposed components—region-level affine supervision (which eliminates fragile point-tracking), gradient mask-based hard constraints for background preservation, and adapter-enhanced inversion—are well-integrated and specifically address the unique characteristics of DiT architectures.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: The method is validated against nine competitive baselines across both DragBench-DR and the newly curated ReD Bench. The paper also includes thorough ablations, such as an exhaustive layer-wise study across all 57 layers of FLUX, a controlled comparison of point vs. region supervision on DiT, and generalizability checks on SD3.5.
weaknesses: High computational latency: DragFlow requires approximately 159 seconds per edit and 23.5 GB peak VRAM (even with INT8 quantization), which significantly limits the interactivity of the user experience compared to faster, lightweight diffusion editing workflows.

Assumptions and limitations of affine supervision: The core mechanism relies on parameterized affine transforms (relocation, rotation, deformation). While effective for rigid and semi-rigid objects, complex non-rigid manipulations or 3D view changes cannot be fully modeled by 2D affine approximations, and editing quality degrades when initial user masks are incomplete or undersized.

Increased interaction complexity via MLLM dependency: Incorporating an MLLM (e.g., GPT-5) to generate candidate prompts and requiring user confirmation across multiple guesses adds external API dependency and friction to what is conventionally a purely visual, point-driven editing interface.

strengths: Timely and insightful analysis: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated analysis of why classic point-based drag editing methods fail on modern Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). Specifically, it highlights the difference in receptive fields and feature compression between UNet bottlenecks and patchified DiT representations, as well as the inversion drift in CFG-distilled models like FLUX.

Well-designed technical framework: The proposed solutions directly target the identified failure modes: progressive region-level affine supervision circumvents brittle point tracking on high-frequency DiT features; hard gradient-mask constraints prevent background degradation during flow matching inversion; and adapter-enhanced inversion restores subject identity.

Comprehensive and thorough empirical evaluation: The paper conducts extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks (DragBench-DR and the newly curated ReD Bench), comparing against nine prior methods. Furthermore, the ablations are exceptionally thorough—including layer-wise feature analysis across all 57 layers, point vs. region comparisons on DiT, MLLM prompt effects, and generalization to SD 3.5.

High visual fidelity: Qualitative results clearly illustrate that leveraging FLUX priors with the proposed regional supervision significantly reduces unnatural artifacts and distortions that commonly plague Stable Diffusion-based draggers.
weaknesses: High computational cost and latency: Drag-based editing is inherently designed for interactive workflows. Table 6 reveals that DragFlow requires ~158.7 seconds per edit and 23.5 GB peak VRAM (even with int8 quantization), which is drastically slower than previous methods (e.g., FastDrag at 5.4s, RegionDrag at 9.2s). This significantly hampers practical interactivity.

Complex multi-component pipeline: The complete system requires multiple auxiliary modules, including an MLLM (e.g., GPT-5 / Qwen-VL) for task classification and prompt generation, a 'double confirmation' user-in-the-loop step, and an external personalization adapter (InstantCharacter / IP-Adapter). This multi-stage dependency adds operational complexity.

Parametric limitations of the affine assumption: Mask propagation relies heavily on 2D affine transformations (translation, rotation). While the authors demonstrate compositions for deformation, handling arbitrary non-rigid topological deformations or fine-grained organic bending remains constrained by this formulation.

Baseline capacity disparity: Most baselines in Table 2 are built upon much smaller SD 1.5/2.1 UNet backbones (~1B parameters), whereas DragFlow uses FLUX.1-dev (~12B parameters). While Table 4 properly ablates point vs. region supervision within DiT, comparing FLUX-based outputs directly to SD-based baselines naturally introduces an inherent visual quality gap due to model capacity alone.

strengths: Clear and insightful motivation: The paper provides a compelling analysis of why conventional point-based drag editing fails when directly ported to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). Specifically, it highlights the mismatch between the narrow receptive fields of fine-grained DiT representations and sparse point-based tracking/supervision, as well as the inversion drift in CFG-distilled models.

Well-designed technical solution: Replacing brittle point tracking with progressive region-level affine supervision neatly sidesteps error accumulation during latent optimization. Furthermore, incorporating adapter-enhanced inversion (via IP-Adapter/InstantCharacter) effectively compensates for subject drift in rectified flow models.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The submission includes an exhaustive layer-wise ablation across all 57 layers of FLUX (Fig. 9), detailed module ablations (Tab. 3), baseline comparisons across two benchmarks, and cross-architecture generalization to SD 3.5 (Tab. 7).

Introduction of ReD Bench: The newly curated benchmark offers paired point- and region-level annotations, explicit task categories (relocation, deformation, rotation), and intent prompts, providing a useful resource for future research in interactive regional editing.
weaknesses: High computational cost and latency: As shown in Table 6, DragFlow requires ~159 seconds per edit and 23.5 GB peak VRAM even with int8 quantization. For an interactive editing tool, this latency significantly impairs real-time usability compared to existing methods running in seconds.

Pipeline complexity and heavy reliance on external components: The complete editing pipeline depends on multiple disparate systems—a heavy DiT backbone (FLUX), an iterative flow inversion solver (FireFlow), an external identity personalization adapter (InstantCharacter / IP-Adapter), and a multimodal LLM (GPT-5) with a human-in-the-loop confirmation step. This makes deployment and reproduction noticeably more complex.

Rigidity of affine mask propagation: The motion supervision relies on 2D affine transformations (translation and rotation) to propagate the operational mask over optimization steps. While the paper touches on complex non-rigid deformation (Sec. C.3 and H.2), large non-affine deformations or topological changes may violate this assumption, leading to potential failure or boundary artifacts.

Baseline comparison disparity: In the primary benchmark comparison (Table 2), all competing baselines are grounded on earlier Stable Diffusion (UNet-based) backbones. While Table 4 provides a comparison against a point-based DiT baseline, evaluating or adapting stronger competitors within the same DiT regime would further isolate the gains attributable to the proposed supervision vs. the underlying base model's capacity.
